summary: Extends RFC 1958 with philosophical guidelines for architects and designers of Internet backbone networks. It describes the Simplicity Principle, which holds that complexity is the main thing that prevents efficient scaling, and discusses what that means for design and engineering of large backbones.

eli5.summary: The big idea is keep it simple. The more complicated a network is, the harder it is to make it bigger, so designers should prefer plain, simple designs.

questions: what is the cell tax in ip over atm
is packet switching simpler than circuit switching
subtitle: Why keeping backbone networks simple matters more than squeezing out features, layers and optimizations.

tldr.problem: Large Internet backbones get more costly and fragile as designers add layers, features and optimizations, and the cost of that complexity is poorly understood.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC argues from the Simplicity Principle: complexity is the primary thing that impedes efficient scaling. It applies this to layering, convergence layers, interworking functions, packet versus circuit switching, over-provisioning and component counts.
tldr.outcome: It concludes that large packet networks must strive for the simplest possible solutions, and that the best convergence layer may be lower in the stack than commonly believed. It extends RFC 1958.

facts.label: Outages from people or process errors

today: RFC 3439 is an Informational document from December 2002 that updates RFC 1958. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Extending RFC 1958
sections.content:
RFC 1958 described the underlying principles of Internet architecture. RFC 3439 extends it with philosophical guidelines for architects and designers of Internet backbone networks. The authors expect many points to be controversial, but not the unifying one: controlling complexity controls costs and reliability.

They quote a line that complexity in most systems is driven by the need for robustness to uncertainty far more than by basic functionality, and say the goal is to raise awareness of how complex current architectures are and what that will do to the IP carrier industry's ability to succeed.
sections.eli5: An older note said how the Internet is built. This one adds advice for the people building its biggest roads: keep things simple.

sections.title: The Simplicity Principle
sections.content:
The Simplicity Principle, perhaps first articulated by Mike O'Dell, says complexity is the primary mechanism that impedes efficient scaling, and so drives up both capital expenditure (CAPEX) and operational expenditure (OPEX). Carrier IP networks should therefore be driven toward the simplest possible solutions.

It links to the end-to-end argument: state belongs in the endpoints and the IP layer, the thin waist of the hourglass, should stay as simple as possible. That does not mean the core holds no state; it holds a lot of coarse-grained state such as routing state, which is almost orthogonal to what hosts keep. This is why protocols like NAT, which reduce transparency between network and hosts, deserve scrutiny.

The RFC also describes ADE non-linearity, behavior that appears only in very large networks, based on two principles:

  • Amplification: small perturbations can have huge effects at large scale. The RFC cites findings that more interconnection makes BGP convergence more complex and often slower, and recommends that local changes have only local effect.
  • Coupling: larger systems have more interdependence between components, horizontally within a layer and vertically across layers. Synchronization of control loops, such as routing updates and TCP Slow Start, is an example, and injecting randomness is one way to reduce it.

It adds that the voice carriers of the 1970s and 1980s added features that made the telephone network more complex, and that adding a new Internet service only requires distributing an application to the consenting desktops.
sections.eli5: A tiny wobble in a huge tower can topple it, and parts that depend on each other tend to fail together. Fewer parts and fewer links between them mean fewer surprises.

sections.title: Layering Considered Harmful
sections.content:
Layers bring structure, but each layer must finish its work before passing data on, so layers are optimized separately and can hide information that others need. Layers may duplicate each other, such as hop-by-hop versus end-to-end error recovery. The RFC concludes that increased layering frequently raises complexity and OPEX, and that horizontal separation may be more cost-effective than vertical separation. It likewise calls optimization and feature richness harmful, because they add complexity and tighter coupling.

It sketches the evolution of IP transport as IP over ATM over SONET, then IP over SONET over WDM, then IP over WDM, with layers removed and CAPEX and OPEX falling. Proposals to put everything over one convergence layer (conduit, DWDM, fiber, ATM, MPLS or IP) are expected to raise OPEX too.

The worked example is the ATM cell tax. On a DS3 line at 44.736 Mbps, after 4.032 for PLCP overhead, 3.840 for cell headers and 5.900 for SNAP header and padding, 30.960 Mbps is left, about 31% total overhead. A 40-byte TCP ACK needs two cells and 106 bytes. The RFC also lists TCP assumptions that lower layers can break: that loss means congestion, that reordering means congestion, that round-trip time signals loss, and that all packets in a flow are treated alike.

It advises avoiding a universal interworking function, and restricting interworking to the data plane and encapsulations done at the network edge, because control plane interworking tends to achieve the worst of all possible worlds.
sections.eli5: If a letter must be put in envelope after envelope, each with its own stamp and label, a lot of paper is wasted. Fewer wrappers means less waste.

sections.title: Packet Versus Circuit Switching
sections.content:
Conventional wisdom says packet switching is more efficient and simpler than circuit switching. The RFC tests this and finds a different picture.

On utilization, it cites reports of average IP link utilization between 3% and 20%, against about 33% for long-haul voice lines. On complexity, it compares a typical Internet router with a transport switch using several metrics (see the table): software size, line-card gates, memory, and power and density, where transport switches use less power and are denser.

The RFC says the underlying driver is hop-by-hop independence (HBHI) in IP, in contrast with end-to-end architectures such as ATM or Frame Relay. It also makes debugging a large IP network demanding. Its conclusion is that packet switching is more complex than circuit switching, and that normalized OPEX for data networks is typically significantly greater than for voice. It admits that no agreed quantitative metrics for network complexity exist.
sections.eli5: A busy post office sorting every letter by hand needs far more machinery than a train that runs on a fixed schedule. Packet networks are the post office.

sections.title: Over-Provisioning, Five Nines and Component Counts
sections.content:
The RFC calls the idea of over-provisioning a misnomer. Keeping utilization below 50% leaves protection capacity, effectively 1:1 protection at the IP layer, similar to a typical SONET network. The benefits are close to speed-of-light delay and close to zero packet loss, and congested packet networks with in-band control loops can become unstable.

It calls five nines reliability for individual network elements a myth. Since 80% of unscheduled outages are blamed on people or process errors, adding complexity to improve components raises the chance of such errors. A system like the Internet can reach five-nines-like reliability, but it is undesirable and likely impossible to make each complex component reach it.

Finally it states the Architectural Component Proportionality Law: complexity is proportional to the number of components, and the probability of a stable implementation is inversely proportional to that number. The corollary is to minimize the components in a service delivery path. As evidence, it says TINA-based and CORBA/TINA-based service architectures had not found a market because their service delivery paths were too complex.
sections.eli5: Leaving a road half empty is not wasteful, because the empty half is what keeps traffic flowing when something goes wrong. And a chain with fewer links is less likely to break.

sections.title: Security and Simplicity
sections.content: The document does not directly affect the security of any existing Internet protocol. The RFC does argue that following the Simplicity Principle improves the ability to build secure systems: as complexity grows, a system becomes harder to model and analyze, and so harder to find and understand its security implications in architecture, design and implementation.
sections.eli5: It is easier to check that a house is locked if it has only a few doors and windows.
